transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Osei, thank you for coming back in to see us. I have Dr. Miller here with me as well.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm a bit confused why you needed me to come back so quickly after we just left.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is an unexpected interruption to your day. This is a difficult conversation to have, but we found a mistake in how we handled your son's vaccinations.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What exactly happened?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: When we were preparing the doses, the medication was drawn up based on a weight band for an older, heavier child. This means your son received a dose of one of the vaccines that was higher than what is indicated for his specific weight.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm sorry, a higher dose? You're telling me he was overdosed because someone didn't check the chart?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was an error in the preparation process. I'm sorry for any confusion this causes. We were incredibly busy in the clinic this morning and the wrong vial was selected.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: As a nurse practitioner, I find that an incredibly disappointing explanation. Being busy doesn't excuse a failure in basic medication safety protocols. This is a fundamental professional standard.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Do you understand the clinical implications of this, or are you just saying that?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The dosage was higher than intended, but it is still within a range that we monitor.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is a very vague answer. I want to know exactly what the risk is for my child right now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can tell you that based on the pharmacology of this specific vaccine, we don't expect any long-term toxicity.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not talking about long-term toxicity. I'm talking about the fact that a safety check was missed. This is a systemic failure.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I see.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're just sitting there. Are you not concerned that your process allowed this to happen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I recognize that this is upsetting.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Upsetting isn't the word. It's a breach of trust. I trusted your team with my son's health.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What is the plan to make sure this doesn't happen to another child?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have a very specific plan for us moving forward. First, I have already flagged this incident in our internal reporting system so the clinic manager can review the dosing workflow. Second, I am going to call our toxicology consult service right now to get a second opinion on any specific monitoring we need for your son. I will call you by 5:00 PM today with their specific feedback.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what about my son's immediate symptoms?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want you to monitor his temperature every four hours for the next twenty-four hours. If he develops a fever over 101 or any unusual rash, I want you to call my personal pager immediately, which I will give to you on a slip of paper before you leave. I am also scheduling a follow-up appointment for him in three days from now to do a physical assessment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I expect a written copy of this incident report.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will provide a formal letter detailing the error, the dose given, and the steps we are taking to prevent this from recurring. I will have that drafted and emailed to your portal by tomorrow morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I still can't get past the "busy" comment. In my practice, "busy" is where the errors happen, but it is never the excuse.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I suppose the plan for the child is comprehensive. But the accountability is missing here.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will make sure the documentation is thorough.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'll wait for that phone call at five. Please make sure you actually speak to the specialist.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will. I will call you at 5:00 PM exactly.

H.justification: The resident never interrupts the patient, remains regulated despite significant pushback, and allows the patient to lead the emotional pace.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly and in lay language, but the resident never performed a comprehension check.

A.justification: While the resident says 'I'm sorry', the apology is diluted by an immediate excuse ('We were incredibly busy in the clinic this morning').

R.justification: The resident relies on generic validations such as 'I understand', 'I see', and 'I hear you' without naming specific emotions.

T.justification: The plan includes specific next steps (toxicology consult, monitoring), clear timelines (5:00 PM, tomorrow morning), a named patient role (monitor temperature), and prevention (internal reporting system).
